plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic of a single array drawn as a long horizontal strip of equal cells, shaded to mark off four regions. Four italic labels sit above the strip: p over the leftmost cell, i over the fourth cell, j further to the right, and r over the rightmost cell. Three heavy black bars stand between cells as the region boundaries. The four cells from p through i are pale gray; the six cells between the first and second bar are a darker gray; the five cells after the second bar and before the last are white and empty; and the single cell at the right end, under r, is white and holds the italic letter x. Three curly braces beneath the strip label the pale gray stretch as at most x, written with the symbol for less than or equal to followed by x, the dark gray stretch as greater than x, and the white stretch as unrestricted. The shading separates the portion of the array already classified against the pivot from the portion not yet examined. The strip states the invariant holding at the top of each iteration while a subarray is rearranged in place around the pivot value stored at position r.

demo_steps.title: Read the invariant
demo_steps.narration: At the top of the loop, everything up to i is already known to be ≤ x, everything from i+1 through j-1 is known to be > x, and everything from j through r-1 has not yet been examined.

demo_steps.title: When A[j] is small enough
demo_steps.narration: If the current element is ≤ x, it belongs in the left region. PARTITION first expands that region by one position, then swaps A[j] into it.

demo_steps.title: When A[j] is too large
demo_steps.narration: If the current element is > x, it already belongs in the middle region. No swap is needed; advancing j simply grows the > x region by one cell.

demo_steps.title: Place the pivot
demo_steps.narration: After every non-pivot element has been classified, the pivot swaps into position i+1. That position separates the final ≤ x region from the final > x region.

plan.keyInsight: The moving boundary j discovers elements, while i marks the end of the ≤ x region; the invariant is restored after every iteration by either swapping a small element left or simply advancing past a large one.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as a long, flat, textbook-style array strip with black outlines and equal cells. Use pale gray for A[p..i], darker gray for A[i+1..j-1], white for A[j..r-1], and a white pivot cell at the far right containing italic x. Labels p, i, j, and r should appear in large italic serif math style above the strip, with thick black vertical markers at the region boundaries. Curly braces under the first three regions should update as i and j move and retain the labels ≤ x, > x, and unrestricted. During code replay, show numeric array values inside the cells while keeping the same region shading so learners can connect the abstract invariant to the concrete swaps.
